notes.b: Being without a job is not the same as being unemployed. The word has a precise meaning, and the effects that follow depend on how long a person is out of work and why.
points: Unemployment means being available for and willing to work, and actively seeking work, but having no paid job. Students, full-time carers and retired people are not counted as unemployed because they are not seeking work.
Long-term unemployment means being out of work for 12 months or more. The longer it lasts, the more damaging it becomes, because savings run out and skills fade.
People lose work for different reasons, for example when a business closes, an industry declines or work is only available at certain times of year.
Unemployment black spots are areas where many people are out of work for a long time, often after a major employer closes, so whole communities feel the loss together.
notes.tip: If asked to define unemployment, include 'seeking work': that is what separates unemployed people from students, carers and retired people.

notes.b: A job gives a person income, status, routine and company. Losing it can damage all four, and the harm usually grows the longer the person is out of work.
points: Financially, loss of income means a lower standard of living and difficulty paying for food, clothing, heating, and rent or mortgage, which can lead to debt.
Psychologically, losing a job can mean losing status, identity and daily routine, so a person may suffer low self-esteem and confidence, boredom and a sense of failure.
Unemployment is linked with stress, anxiety and depression (mental health problems), especially when money worries and rejected job applications build up.
Health and behaviour can suffer: physical health may be poorer, and some people turn to alcohol, drugs or gambling to cope, which adds to financial and health problems.
Socially, a person loses workplace contacts and friends, and has less social life because going out costs money, so isolation and loss of motivation can follow.
Skills become out of date, and a gap in the CV makes employers less likely to hire, so long-term unemployment feeds on itself and makes finding work harder.
Young people lose the chance to gain work experience, which delays independence: they may stay living with their parents and find it hard to move out.
Young people may be tempted to emigrate to find work, and some are at risk of antisocial behaviour when they have no job or routine.
notes.tip: Exams ask for effects on the individual, the family and society as separate levels. Give each effect one sentence of explanation and place it at the right level.

notes.b: When one person loses their job, the whole household feels it. Money, relationships, roles and children are all affected, though how badly depends on how long the unemployment lasts and how much support the family has.
points: Lower income means a reduced standard of living, cuts to savings, holidays, clothes and activities, and debt, with mortgage or rent arrears that can put the home at risk.
Families may rely on credit or moneylenders, social welfare payments and help from MABS to manage, but borrowing can make the money problem worse.
Financial strain causes arguments between partners and can lead to relationship breakdown, because stress and tension build up, and in some families to violence or addiction.
Roles can reverse: a parent who loses the job may become the main carer at home, which can reduce their status and authority in the family.
The other partner may have to work longer hours or take work they would not choose, to make up the lost income.
Children may have a poorer diet, miss school trips, school costs, activities and leisure, and show stress and behaviour problems because of the tension at home.
Older children may leave education early or choose a college by cost rather than by what they want to study.
Children in long-term unemployed households may lack working adults as role models, which makes it harder for them to see work as normal.
notes.tip: Do not list only negatives. Say that effects vary with the length of unemployment, the family's savings and support, and the cause (redundancy against seasonal work).

notes.b: Unemployment can pull a family apart physically, as people leave to find work, though it can also give some families more time with one another.
points: Family members may emigrate or move to find work. This splits families, leaves older relatives without support and reduces the population of the community they leave.
More time together can be a positive effect, since a parent at home can spend more time with the children and do household tasks, but this is usually outweighed by stress.
notes.tip: On emigration for work, discuss the impact on both the individual and the family.

notes.h: Effects on society and the community
notes.b: Unemployment is not only a private problem. When many people are out of work, the State, the local economy and the community all pay a price.
points: The State spends more on social welfare while it collects less income tax and PRSI, because fewer people are earning, so there is less money for public services.
Households with less income spend less, so local shops and businesses suffer and more jobs can be put at risk.
Loss of skills and productive effort reduces output and economic growth, and emigration of skilled people (brain drain) takes talent away from the country.
Concentrations of unemployment cause social exclusion and unemployment black spots, where people are cut off from the opportunities most others have.
Poverty, crime, vandalism and antisocial behaviour can increase in areas of high unemployment.
High unemployment puts strain on health, mental health and other services, and contributes to family breakdown and homelessness.
Emigration can cause depopulation of areas, and a weaker community spirit follows when people, clubs and services leave.
notes.tip: For a question on effects on society, cover welfare cost, lost tax, lost output, crime, black spots and emigration, with a sentence of explanation for each.

notes.b: Statutory schemes are run by the State and paid for by taxes. They replace some lost income and help people get back to work.
points: The Department of Social Protection runs the income supports and operates its public employment service as Intreo.

Jobseeker's Benefit is a social insurance payment based on PRSI contributions, paid for a limited period. Jobseeker's Allowance is means-tested, meaning it depends on the person's income and resources.
Supplementary Welfare Allowance meets urgent needs, and the Working Family Payment tops up the income of low-paid workers with children.
A statutory redundancy payment is paid to eligible employees who are made redundant, under the Redundancy Payments Acts.
The Back to Education Allowance gives income support to people on certain social welfare payments while they take approved second or third level courses.

SOLAS (which took over from the earlier training body in 2013) and the Education and Training Boards provide further education and training, and Springboard+ offers courses to help people return to work.
Community Employment and Tús are temporary work placements in communities that give work experience, and Youthreach helps young early school leavers.
notes.tip: Name the scheme (about 4 marks), say who it helps, and give two details of what it provides. A statutory scheme is State-run and paid for by taxes, so do not confuse it with a voluntary organisation.

notes.h: Information, money advice and voluntary organisations
notes.b: Not all help comes from the State. Free advice services and charities support unemployed families, often with the practical problems that the payments do not cover.
points: Citizens Information is a free, impartial information service that tells people what payments and services they are entitled to.
MABS, the Money Advice and Budgeting Service, gives free, confidential help with debt and household budgeting, so families can manage on a reduced income.
The Society of St Vincent de Paul (SVP) is a voluntary charity with local conferences and charity shops. It helps with bills, food, school costs and housing, and visits families.
The Irish National Organisation of the Unemployed (INOU) is a national network that gives advice, advocacy and information to unemployed people.
Local community and family resource centres also offer support close to home.
Voluntary work benefits the unemployed person by giving structure, skills, contacts and confidence, and it benefits the community through the help given.
notes.tip: A voluntary organisation is a charity run by volunteers, such as SVP or INOU. Name it, say who it helps, and give two details of what it provides.

notes.h: Applying it: a family where a parent loses a job
notes.b: Exam questions often describe a family and ask you to apply what you know, so practise working through each member in turn.
points: Start with the parent who lost the job: loss of income, status and routine, stress, and the risk of skills becoming out of date.
Then the partner, who may work longer or take work they would not choose, and the couple, whose relationship is under financial strain.
Then the children, who may miss trips and activities, have a poorer diet and feel stress at home.

Finish with the supports the family could use: a Jobseeker's payment through Intreo, MABS for money problems, Citizens Information for entitlements, the SVP for practical help, and the Back to Education Allowance or a training course for a route back to work.
notes.tip: Say who in the family is affected and how, and match each problem to a named support. Effects vary with how long the unemployment lasts and how much savings and support the family has.

keyTerms.definition: The condition of people who are available for and willing to work but do not have paid employment.
Short-term unemployment that occurs while people move between jobs or enter the labour market.
Unemployment caused by lasting changes in the economy, such as new technology or the decline of an industry.
Unemployment that rises during economic recessions when demand for goods and services falls.
Unemployment in industries whose work depends on the time of year.
Being out of work for a year or more while looking for work.
A change in family roles in which a parent takes on the caring tasks and the other partner loses a traditional role.
Payments that are overdue, such as unpaid rent, mortgage repayments or utility bills.

factCards.term: Four effects of unemployment on the individual
factCards.definition: Loss of income, loss of status, stress or depression, and social isolation.
A lower standard of living and poorer diet, missed school and leisure activities, and fewer working role models.

factCards.term: Two state supports for unemployed families
factCards.definition: Social welfare income support and free debt advice from MABS.

questions.prompt: Name two effects of unemployment on family finances.
questions.model: Loss of income makes it hard to pay mortgage or rent and bills, leading to arrears and debt. Spending on food, clothing and leisure has to be cut. Savings are used up, or the family must borrow.

questions.prompt: Analyse how long-term unemployment affects a family's finances, relationships and children, and describe one support that helps families cope.
questions.model: Finances: loss of income leads to arrears on rent or mortgage, debt, reduced spending on essentials and leisure, and reliance on savings or credit. Relationships: financial strain causes arguments and can lead to relationship breakdown; a parent who becomes the main carer at home may lose authority or status, and roles can reverse. Children: they may miss school trips and activities, face a poorer diet on a tight budget, and lack working adults as role models for employment. Family members may have to move or emigrate to find work. Support: social welfare income support gives a regular income to those who meet the conditions; MABS gives free help with debt and budgeting; Citizens Information explains entitlements; the Back to Education Allowance helps unemployed people take approved courses.
